learning_objective: 🎯 Dig deep into India's geological wealth! Learn about the minerals that build our industries and the fuels that power our nation.

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Minerals are divided into Metallic (ferrous like iron/manganese, and non-ferrous like copper/bauxite) and Non-metallic (like mica and limestone).
Minerals are unevenly distributed. The North-Eastern Plateau region (Chotanagpur) is the richest mineral belt, often called the 'Ruhr of India'.
Traditional, exhaustible power sources like Coal (Gondwana and Tertiary coal), Petroleum (Digboi, Mumbai High), and Natural Gas. They cause pollution and are running out.
Clean, renewable future energy! Includes Solar power, Wind energy (huge potential in Gujarat/Tamil Nadu), Hydroelectric, Geothermal, and Biomass.
Minerals take millions of years to form. We must use them sustainably, recycle metals, and shift aggressively towards renewable energy sources.

fun_activity.title: 🔗 Household Mining
fun_activity.instructions: Find 5 items in your house and identify the minerals used in them! (e.g., Wires = Copper, Utensils = Iron/Aluminum, Talcum powder = Talc, Pencil = Graphite).

exam_tips: 📌 Always locate Mumbai High (petroleum), Mayurbhanj (iron ore), and Khetri (copper) on your map practice.
📌 Distinguish between Ferrous and Non-ferrous minerals with examples.
📌 Justify why non-conventional energy is essential for sustainable development in India.
quick_recap: ⭐ Chotanagpur plateau is famous for its massive reserves of coal and iron ore.
⭐ India is highly deficient in reserves of copper and petroleum, heavily relying on imports.
⭐ Nuclear energy requires uranium and thorium, which are found in Rajasthan and Kerala coasts.
